Positioning

Joined-up leads. Trust is the on-ramp.

When a partner weighs us up, they’re rarely choosing between us and another full-stack agency. They’re weighing us against a cheaper or more familiar alternative — and all of those alternatives are really one objection wearing different clothes.

Doing it themselves

“Why pay an agency at all?”

Don’t trust an agency to beat what they do in-house.

Single-channel people

“I trust this one narrow thing.”

An ads guy or SEO person — not a big agency promise.

In-house hire

“I’d rather control my own person.”

Especially live for bigger businesses weighing a salary.

Burned by an agency

“I tried trusting one and got hurt.”

Huge in performance marketing — the deepest trust deficit.

Underneath, they’re the same: “I don’t believe an agency will actually deliver.” Which is why our positioning works in a specific order:

Joined-up / full-stack is the lead — it’s what genuinely makes us different. Most agencies sit in one lane; we connect the channels so each makes the others perform better. Trust-first is the on-ramp — it’s what gets a sceptical partner to believe the lead is real. For a burned prospect we lead with the on-ramp; for everyone else we lead with joined-up and trust does its work underneath.

They didn’t need ‘more marketing.’ They needed joined-up marketing.The AG Osteopathy insight

The partner journey

Enter on the problem. Integrate until we run it all.

However a partner comes in, they travel the same spine: enter on the priority fix, prove it works, pass a gate, then expand. The loop repeats until they reach the full-stack end state — where their only involvement is input and approvals.

The gate is the most important mechanic here. Expansion is results-gated, not time-gated — we never pitch the next layer until we’ve earned it with the last one. Liam’s reporting surfaces the win; Fee owns spotting the gate and opening the next conversation.

From entry to full-stack

The commercial engine

How the model makes money.

The journey shows the story; this is the economics. A single account layers three different revenue mechanics over time — and crucially, two of them grow without us selling anything new.

One-off

Project fees

Bespoke builds, rebrands, production days. The entry spike on project-led partners.

Recurring

Retainers

Monthly management & engine fees. The prize — predictable revenue that ramps as we cross-sell.

Scaling

Ad-spend commission

Tiered 8–14%. As we make their ads work and budgets grow, our cut climbs — revenue grows even if we sell nothing new.

The cross-sell ladder (see the journey) is what stacks these. AG entered on a single Google Ads retainer and twelve months later was an eight-channel account — recurring revenue ramping from one line item to a full stack, with commission compounding alongside as spend grew. The CRVs protect the entry point: the paid audit is a de-risked paid start, content days buy access to high-value accounts.

Reference rates — from current proposals

Meta / Google Ads management ~£850/mo each · Organic Content Engine £1,300/mo · unlimited Design / Tech / Video Editing £500/mo each · Social Scheduling £300/mo · production day £1,400 one-off · ad-spend commission 8–14% · paid audit £1,250 (credited against execution) · £2,000 first-30-day fee on performance retainers.

Engagement ladder

Leave no money on the table. If there’s no money, leave a relationship.

Our governing commercial rule. We always try to land as high up this ladder as possible, dropping down only as far as we must. Only genuine red flags end the relationship.

  1. Retainer or projectThe prize — recurring revenue or a phased build.
  2. Paid auditThe minimum paid engagement. Our “at least get this” fallback.
  3. Free assetNo money now? Give value (e.g. an AI-generated audit/asset) to stay in the game and plant a future seed.
  4. Clarity + future follow-upNot a fit yet? Tell them honestly why, so they can become one later. Keep the door open.
  5. No further contactReserved only for genuine red flags — bad character, not a nice person. The one true dead end.

Lead generation

Five engines, one conversation.

We get into conversations five different ways. They all converge on the same point — a qualifying, trust-building conversation — which then resolves into one of two routes in.

Direct sell is the preferred outcome; the commercial release valves (CRVs) are the fallback. The two are interchangeable in order — we try the front door first and drop to a side door only when we need to. And note the loop: existing full-stack partners feed cross-sells back into the outreach engine, so the business feeds itself.

Front of the funnel
The two routes are interchangeable; direct sell is preferred, CRVs are the fallback. Existing partners are themselves a lead source.

Three tiers & how we handle them

Strategic partners to define together

The ecosystem we’re formalising.

A referral ecosystem with anyone who shares our ideal partner but sells something we don’t — PR agencies, single-channel agencies, business consultants, accountants, chambers of commerce. Mutual benefit: the partner gets a better overall result. Live but informal today — we have named relationships and ad-hoc referrals, but no structured programme yet.

Two things to settle

The reciprocity question. This only works if value flows both ways. The open question is what we give partners that makes them want to send us their best clients — the bit most agency partner programmes miss.

The prey-vs-partner rule for single-channel players. Single-channel operators are both prey (we replace the lone ads/SEO person as we expand an account) and partner (we refer work to each other). The working line: a freelance/solo single-channel operator is someone we replace; an established single-channel agency with its own client base is someone we partner with.

Open questions for the team
  • What’s the reciprocal offer that makes partners refer to us?
  • Confirm the prey-vs-partner rule for single-channel players.
  • Which named relationships do we formalise first?

why it works

Joined-up beats more.

The reason most marketing underperforms isn’t effort — it’s that the pieces don’t talk to each other. A great ad sends traffic to a weak site. Brilliant content has no system to capture the leads it earns.

We connect every channel so each one makes the others work harder. You see exactly what we see — full visibility, no guesswork, decisions backed by data. And because we start by proving results before we expand, you’re never asked to bet big before you’ve seen it work.
